Freddie Moore (March 30, 1983):

This is the interview with Fred Moore for the Jazz Oral History Project, March 30th, Wednesday, 1983, in the home of Mr. and Mrs. Moore in the Bronx, New York. My name is Ron Welburn, Interviewer. Fred Moore, good morning.
Good morning.
How have you been?
Oh, I've been pretty good for an old man.
Getting along all right, huh?
Yeah. I still have my health and strength. I'm still working three or four nights a week.
Well, that's wonderful that you're able to still be active.
Yeah...
[PAUSE]
Fred Moore, you were born in the year 1900.
Yeah.
What is your date of birth and where were you born?
I was born in Little Washington, North Carolina. My age is, I was born 1900, and my birthday is August the 20th.
August the 20th, 1900.
Moore (I) - 2

I ran away from home when I was fourteen years old, just to try to entertain the people, but I was a little bit too young. I was with this minstrel show for a long time, about...oh, about a couple of years, a year. The A.G. Allen Minstrel Show.
A.G. Allen. Well, Fred, what caused you to run away. I mean, you wanted to get involved in entertainment of some sort?

I wanted to get involvement with entertainment, but I didn't know what it was all about. I loved drums so much. Around the house, I used to hit on the different frying pans, anything I could get a sound from. I used to take the rungs out the old chairs, just whittle them down on the end to make a drumstick.
How did your mother feel about that and your father?
She wasn't too happy. My father wasn't living then.
I see.

My father died when I was very young. I think my father died when I was around nine weeks, nine months old or something like that. I don't remember, it's been so long, but... But my mother wasn't too happy about me making all that noise in the house, you know.
Moore (I) - 3

So I got an opportunity to join this minstrel show. But I joined the minstrel show, but I wasn't... I wasn't able to play drums, because I was... They hired me for a walking gent, to hang the coats up on the bushes or the trees when the band would make the parade and go downtown...
Whose coats would you be hanging up there? The band members'?

The band. The band uniforms. They had a six-piece band, and they had six coats, red coats. And it would get awful sweaty, awfully hot down South, especially at that time of the year. They used to hang them up on there when they'd come in from the parade, and they'd dry in about an hour and a half. After they dried, then I'd take them and put them on the coat hangers and put them in their car. They had a Pullman car there. I'd put them in the car and hang them up. And in the next town, when we'd get in, it would be all dry. So we used the same uniform again.
What color were these uniforms?
Red uniforms.
They had trim on them?
Yeah. They trimmed it with black around the collar and black around the sleeves. Wear it long. Get down probably...almost down to your ankle.
The shoes that the band members wore, were they black shoes or brown shoes?
Some black shoes, some brown shoes.
So there was no... It didn't matter...
It didn't matter during that time. Just the coats.
I see. And the hats... They had hats?
Well, sometimes they'd wear a hat or a cap, or a cap, or any kind of hat that... Caps, mostly caps. It wasn't necessary for them to wear a hat.
What kind of music did these bands play as they marched through the streets?
Well, they played numbers, like... Regular March numbers, like a lot of Souza...Souza marches. [SINGS...]
'Stars and Stripes Forever.'
Yeah, a number like that. And... Everything a march, you know. Well, I didn't know anything about... When they sang(?) to a march in (?), I didn't know anything about that. We didn't play that.
Were there any numbers that were played kind of like double-time or, say, in a kind of jazzed-up way? Were there any numbers played like that by the band?
Moore (I) - 5
Yes. We played numbers like "Don't Be ...(?)..." They don't play them no more.
Ragtime numbers?
They'd play a number like "Rastus Trombone"...
Oh yeah, "Rastus Trombone."
...and "Slide Trombone." Different numbers. Whatever you'd play, we had a tendency with a beat of three to it...
I see.
Except a march. You couldn't do too much with them. But if you'd get the right tempo, you could make it swing. We'd do a lot of Classical numbers, you know.
Oh, overtures and...?
Yeah, a whole lot of overtures.
"Shores of the Minnetonka," numbers like that?
Numbers like that, yeah.
How about... You did Ragtime numbers also? Some Scott Joplin numbers?
We did quite a few of them.
James Scott... How about Perry Mills' "Georgia Camp Meeting"?
Yeah, numbers like that. [SINGS REFRAIN]
"Creole Bells."
Moore (I) - 6
Yeah, especially lively numbers like that. 'Creole Bells...'
You were playing drums for that marching band... No, you were hanging up the coats.
The walking gent, hang the coats up.
But what was the instrumentation of that marching band? You said there were about six...
Bass drum, snare drum, banjo, trombone, clarinet... How many pieces is that?
That's five.
Five...
Was there a cornet player?
Yeah, it had a cornet player.
And that was the basic group.
Yes.
I see. And sometimes you'd add an instrument every once in a while?
It was hard(?) to add on, because that was what you call a real marching band.
I see.
It had a clarinet, tuba, and sometimes it used baritone...
Baritone horn.
Moore (I) - 7

Yeah, a baritone horn. That's going to seven pieces. Six or seven pieces. Most of them used baritone horn, bass, trombone, clarinet and trumpet -- and the banjo. So you've got a banjo in that. It had to replace the piano. The banjo played the chords right...it had to play the right chords.
I see. Do you remember the names of some of these musicians who were playing? This is A.G. Allen's...
A.G. Allen's Minstrel.
Do you remember the names of some of these musicians?
I only can remember the leader's name. We called him Professor Booker.
Professor Booker.
Professor Booker. He was the bandleader. he was a trumpet player. The baritone player was named Jazz Curry.
Jazz Curry.
Yeah, Jazz Curry. He was a baritone player. The rest of them I can't remember...
About how old were you when you were...? You were about fourteen or fifteen?
Oh, I must have been around...
Or you were a little older.
Moore (I) - 8

Fourteen or fifteen years old. Now, I left home when I was fourteen. Before... Well, I got started at home... I used to... A place called the Frog Pond. I used to go down to the Frog Pond; they had a dance hall upstairs -- just piano-drums. I had to give the boy 25 cents during intermission. They let me set up all the drums, and I played a little bit on the drums. I didn't know what I was doing. I just rode the rhythm, you know.

I was interested in the name that this fellow had, "Jazz," and if it was around, say, 1915 do you think, or 1916, before the United States got involved in the First World War...? Do you think it was that early?
About 1916.

I see. It's interesting that he would have the name Jazz, when not very many instances, apparently, of the use of the name of Jazz or the word "Jazz" were apparent at that time, or at least according to what we have known so far. That's an interesting little bit of historical information.
Let's back up a bit, Fred, and talk about your mother and father and your grandparents. Your mother worked around the home. Were her parents living?
I think she had about one or two... Her uncle, his name was... Her last name was Cherry(?), but I was so
Moore (I) - 9

young to know what... My mother used to take in washing and ironing to keep us...to help raise us, you know. She did that kind of... There was two or three of us, myself and my brother Eddie. Of course, I was the youngest one. I was about, oh, three or four years older [sic] than my brother. That's the only one who's living, is my brother -- he's living in North Carolina. I guess he must be now around 85 years old.
And you are the youngest.
I'm the youngest.
So there were three boys altogether, and no girls...
Yes.
No sisters.
Myself and Johnny Moore and Eddie Moore, the three boys...,
Yes.
...and two sisters. There was five altogether.
Oh.
Oh yes, there's one more; I forgot to mention his name. A brother next to (?)...Will... His name was Wilmore. He was the oldest one.
Wilmore.
Wilmore. My brother Eddie was next to Wilmore.
Moore (I) - 10
I see. Were any of these siblings involved in music or entertainment? Or were you the only one?
No. I'm the onliest one.
I see. Did you know your father's people, his mother and father?
No, I didn't know none of those. All I know is... I just remember my mother used to tell me this was her husband. His name was Giles. Giles Moore.
Giles Moore.
I don't remember him, I was so young.
Yeah. You were essentially a babe in arms.
Yeah. They said I was around nine weeks old or something around there. Ten weeks old.
Where actually is Little Washington, North Carolina? What are the largest cities and towns in the vicinity?

Well, Little Washington, North Carolina... The reason why they called it Little Washington was to put the... There's a distinction between Little Washington and Washington, North Carolina...Washington, D.C., rather... I always heard that Little Washington wasn't on the map. So I learned later it is on the map, but it's a small town. All of those different towns, cities...I wouldn't call them cities...are not too far apart. You've got Greensboro,
Moore (I) - 11
North Carolina, Charlotte, Raleigh, Roseboro, Winston-Salem... I can't go on...I could go on, but... But the others were smaller places, real small.
I see.
The population I don't know.

When you were a boy, before running away from home, do you recall seeing or hearing any musicians come through town, traveling musicians who may have played Ragtime or other kinds of, say, Cakewalk music?

The only musicians who come through town there was playing... They were playing the same kind of music we was playing. But I just made up my mind I wanted to leave home, run away from home at that age... Around nine, ten, eleven years old, twelve, I had some nights I'd go up to the Frog Pond and sit in on the drums. And they had a little band there. They had some good musicians there in Newbern, North Carolina. But you couldn't get them out of there.
This is Newbern, North Carolina.
Newbern [SPELLS], North Carolina.
Newbern. I see.
They had some very good musicians there. The piano player was Hootie Green. He was one of the greatest piano players around.
Hootie Green.
Moore (I) - 12
Yeah.
And he played a lot of the popular songs of the day?

Yeah. Whatever he played, he had a very good left hand. Something like Fats Waller. He didn't do no singing; he just played. But he always liked good drumming. He had his own drums with him. The drums would be out there. So he told me... He'd been there about ten years, in one place. That's all he used at the Frog Pond.
So the Frog Pond was a dance hall.
A dance hall upstairs.
Was there any playing of music in taverns or bars or any restaurants in any of the nearby cities and towns?

Well, I don't know too much about barroom... I don't think too many bars was open during that time. I remember, I used to go out on the street and pick up bottles... I guess there must have been barrooms open for it to have them whiskey bottles. I'd go pick up the whiskey bottles, Coca-Cola bottles, and sell them. I used to get two or three cents a bottle for them bottles. Now they call them taverns...I don't know what they call them... They call them bars. I don't think they had the bars during that time... But anyway, I was so young, I wasn't allowed in them
Moore (I) - 13
even if they had them.
I see. So Hootie Green was the big... He was the most well-known musician in that area, I take it.
Yes.
I see. And he had a drummer. Do you recall seeing or hearing other musicians sit in with him at the dance hall? A trumpet player maybe, or a cornet player or clarinet player?
No. I don't remember any of the others. I just remember this particular one.
Hootie Green.
Yeah..
How about singers?
No singers.
Do you recall, Fred, before you left home, any cakewalks where people would dance in order to win the cake? To win the cake. Do you recall any of that?
Something on the order of "Cakewalking Baby"... [HUMS REFRAIN] "Cakewalking Baby." Anything to do in that in the different tempos, they called them cakewalking numbers.
I see.
But this particular number was named Cakewalking Baby." But the other numbers, I don't remember
Moore (I) - 14
now the name of them.

But do you remember any affairs, whether indoor affairs or outside, where there may have been a contest, and the prize of the contest for whoever was the best dancer or the best cakewalker, would win the cake...
Well, they probably had all of that. But I didn't get a chance to see all that.
I see. Okay.
I was so young, a person my age... I think I've done not badly on the (?). I think I've done very good to think. In the teens, up until 83, things have passed, and I think back..
Sure.
Whatever I say is true. I don't make up. I don't pretend. Hear what I say or you say... I say it, that's the way it is.

Oh, no. Well, there's no doubt that you've had a great and productive life. The Oral History Project is interested in this, because there are a number of things that are important to our understanding of the history of entertainment and Jazz, and how it developed in this country.
Now, you were... When you left home, then had you finished school? Had you stopped going to school? Or did
Moore (I) - 15
you leave school also and decide that you didn't want to go back?
I left school. I decided I didn't want to go back. I went to the place for Second and Third Grade. I made the Third Grade; that was it.
I see. And even in school, you were interested in the drums? Was it the sound of the drums or the loudness of the rapping of it, using the chair rungs...?
It was the sound. The sound and the rhythm.
Rhythm.

Sound and the rhythm. When I'd be hittin' on it, it would sound like Chinese, because I'd be hittin' on the tin-pan... [DA-RUNG, DONG, DUNG]... Frying pan, on the chairs... Anything I could get a sound, that was rhythm.
I see. But at that time, you didn't know anything about how to use your wrist, rolls and that sort of thing.
Mmm-hmm.
You were just beating.
I didn't have no drumsticks. What I did have was a... [COUGHS]
[PAUSE]
What I did have, as I said, was the chair, like a chair that you sit in, an old broke-down chairs that wasn't no
Moore (I) - 16
good and Mother had 'em throwed out in the back yard. I'd go out there and get them, and take a cake knife, a knife and a fork...the knife, not the fork...
Sure.
And I'd whittle them down on the end, make me think they was a drumstick, you know... I didn't know anything about rolling or all that stuff.

A question about drumsticks. Of course, you made drumsticks, but you were familiar with what drumsticks looked like at that time. Around the time that you were leaving home, were the drumsticks that were used by drummers larger than they are used now, or, say, the drumsticks that you have now...
Yeah, a little... The drumsticks that they used then was...what you call it...? Military drums, that you use in...
Military.
Yeah, military drums. They didn't use the kind of sticks that we use now. In fact, they didn't make them. What they use now is the plastic tips...
That's right.
Plastic tips. And some is not plastic. The ones that's not plastic, they'll split. You've got a... To the end you've got a (?) with a splinter...what'cha call
Moore (I) - 17
them, splinter...? Like a little chip get in them. I see.
But the plastic don't do that. The plastic sticks, they don't split. They would end up breaking. Finally, in the end, in the (?), it will break. But they won't split.
I see. Do you prefer these plastic tipped drumsticks today as opposed to...?
Yes. Plastic sticks is better. You get a very...a crisp roll. But you got to know how to roll.
Sure. Well, we'll get into some of those things as we go along. What were the sticks years ago made of, when you were a youngster first starting out at the drums?

Pine wood and maple -- maple wood. Some was made out of hickory, hickory wood. But you can't...you can't... It's hard to find. You can't find the hickory sticks no more. The ordinary sticks now that I use cost $3.50 or $4 a pair. If you have the hickory stick, it will cost you round about $6 a pair, $7.

And I didn't know anything about wire brushes during that time. You didn't use no wire brushes. I come to New York, they were using the wire brushes. The wire brushes cost you a dollar and a half a pair during that time. Now
Moore (I) - 18
the same wire brush (they may make them a little bit better; I don't know) can run you from four to five dollars, six dollars a pair, right now.
You gave the prices for drumsticks now. Years ago, what would pine sticks cost?
Fifty cents a pair.
Fifty cents a pair. The rate of inflation.
[CHUCKLES]

Which did you find... Of course, all the drummers had their preferences. Some would like the pine and others would like the hickory. Were there any of the wood types, maple or hickory or pine, that were more popular than others?
Well...
Or was it simply a matter of individual preference all the way down?
Pine wood was... It's a light fit.
It's light.
And the maple sticks is next to it. It's light, too. And the hickory sticks, forget about that -- you couldn't get those at all.
Once you joined A.G. Allen, did you know of drummers you might have encountered who made their own sticks, the way you used to fashion their sticks that may
Moore (I) - 19
No...
They would always go to a music store?

No, there's such a thing as... Some guys used to try to make their sticks. They'd out in the woods, pick up some limbs from the trees the size of the drumsticks, what looked like the size of the drumsticks. They used to whittle them down to the end and take the pine off...the sap off the stick...not the sap, but... I don't know what they would call it. But anyway...
The bark.

Yeah, take the bark off and put resin on them. Put that resin on it and they wouldn't warp during that time. But now the sticks warp. When you go down to buy sticks, man, you've got to get...put them on a counter. The counter is something like a big... A counter, about this wide, you know...
Mmm-hmm.
And they put them on there and roll them. If they roll smooth, it's all right. But if they start looking like that, it ain't no good. It's kind of hard for a drummer to play with a warped stick.
They don't them, apparently, as well as they used to.
Moore (I) - 20
Maybe it's the weather.
The weather?

The weather will make the sticks like that. A lot of them, you get them and you buy them, it's in a plastic kit bag, the plastic bags, small bags, just the size enough of two sticks to go in them. That will help to keep them moist(?)...keep the weather from getting to them. But if the weather, the air gets to them, they've got a tendency to warp.

While we're talking about sticks and equipment, we can say a few things about drum-heads at that time. When we were talking once before, you mentioned that the early drum-heads were made of sort of like cowhide.
Cowhide, calfskin, mostly calfskin.
And were they very expensive for, say, the bass drum and the snare drum?
The snare drum... You never... You'd have to buy them separate. They wasn't mounted. I mean, they wasn't put on a hook.
I see. So you had to do all that yourself.

You had to get your... Say you busted your drumhead. I could put tape on a damaged head, and it would have that sound; it would hold it together, you know. And I used to take a spoon, the end of a spoon, and I used to tuck
Moore (I) - 21

my drum head on this rim. You'd put your... You'd wet the drum head and spin it out, and take this rim, put it right on top of the drum-head. It's something like you wrap it up and take your spoon and tuck it up on there tight. They don't have that no more. They're always on the rim, always mounted. All you got to do is get the drum head and take the screws off and put them right on. So all that's done in about...oh, it's about three or four minutes; inside of five minutes.

I see. When you were with A.G. Allen, I'm sure that you had a chance to see other drummers. Did you notice how they took care of their drums? What kinds of things did they do to keep the drumheads in good shape. And what kinds of things did you do?
Well, they didn't use no... They used them... there were drum covers. That's going back as far as Texas Joe(?), had a thing called a... They used to have a box made especially for your drums...
[END OF TAPE 1, SIDE A]
So you had a box especially made for your drums.
Moore (I) - 22

Yes. Just the size of how your bass pedal is(?). And you put the small stuff down in there; we used to pack it down with an old blanket to keep it from rattling. During that time, they used the big bass drums. They had a 28-inch bass drum. They don't use that no more.
28 inches. That's a good size.
Yeah, 28 inches. You didn't have too much traps to go in there You had the little alligator foot pedal stands(?) down on the floor, and you had this one cymbal stand -- you used about one cymbal.
Why was this called an alligator foot pedal?
Because it laid like an alligator, with its mouth, you know...
I see. This was...
This was down on the floor. During that time, they didn't use no hi-hat.
No hi-hat.
Didn't know anything about the hi-hat. And whoever invented the hi-hat could have made a fortune off it.
He certainly did.
Yeah. I didn't know anything about hi-hats until I came to New York.
Moore (I) - 23
How large was the cymbal that you used or that drummers customarily used around that time, around when you were say a teenager?
The (?) cymbals? Do you mean the hi-hat?
Well, the size of...
On the bass drum?
Yes.
About 12-14-15 inches.
They don't look to be very large according to your pictures.

No. They're a little on the... They're about 12 inches. Probably 14 inches. Some of them maybe 15 inches, but no larger. It wasn't big. But during that time drummers didn't use too much cymbals. They did a lot of press rolls. Whatever you'd do to get a good, solid beat, you'd stay on that snare drum.
So it was all on the snare drum, and also...
Mostly on the snare drum. And you could play on the cymbals, too, if you knew how to play on them.

And the bass drum... During the time that you were a teenager and you were playing drums, you were starting out early, you were watching the other drummers, how they played... Did they use the bass drum, say, a constant beat [RAPS 4-4 TIME] -- something like that?
Moore (I) - 24

Yeah... Well, during that time, some of them used four beats. But what it's supposed to be, the right way is to use two beats. So I used two beats. Right now in fast numbers, the first chorus I use two beats. That's to steady the band, the tempo right there. But after the first half of the first chorus, in the second half of the first chorus, then I start using four beats. Then I keep it up until they finish the number. Fast or slow. I can play it better fast than I could slow. Slow numbers tire me out.
Oh, they can make...

For a fast number, I'm right in there. I know what I'm supposed to do. I keep the tempos up. Don't get no faster, don't get no slower. On most of the songs, I do. Sometimes I'll get a little bit... I'll get the same way, too; I get carried away, you know.
When you were young, starting out as a drummer, if you played, say, two beats as opposed to four beats, were the two beats on, say, two and four, or would they be on one and three, or did it vary?
I used to... When I'm playing four beats...
Well, then, it's four to the bar.
...it sounds like two. And when I'm playing two, it sounds like four. But I accent on my third beat, and the accent on the third beat... Then I'm playing four.
Moore (I) - 25
I see...

Instead of me hitting the bass drum right down solid, I've got a little after-beat on the bass...on the bass drum, which would make it swing better. See, if you hit... When you're playing four, when you hit the bass drum right down the straight, it sounds the same thing. You can't give very much swing to the band, you know.

I see. Well, these are all important things to know here. Well, how far did you have to go to join A.G. Allen's Minstrels? When you decided that you were going to leave home, did you have it in mind that you were going to go to A.G. Allen? Or did you just decide to leave and you were going to hook up with...?

When I started... The first minstrel show, which was (?)... The first minstrel show was about...oh, say, about a mile-and-a-half from my home. I could walk there, you know. So I was talkin' with the man, and he said, "You want a job?" I said, "Yeah." He said, "I'll make you my walking gent." When the band goes on parade, if you want to walk beside the drummer and watch him, all right. But when the band comes back off parade, you have to hang those coats up, let them dry. We'll give you the name of the walking gent." He told me how much they'd pay me. I think it... Well, I started at three dollars a week, just to
Moore (I) - 26
take care of them coats. And eat and sleep, room and board out on the car.
So you had the Pullman cars.

We had a Pullman car. It was holding(?) I'd say about... Say about a five- or six-piece band and about three chorus girls, and a comedian and a dancer, a soubrette... Of course, the boss, he had his own private office right up in the front, the front of the car, you know.
Can you tell me some more about A.G. Allen? What kind of individual was he? Was he easy to get along with?

He was very easy to get along with. He'd never bother you about nothin'. All he'd do, he wanted to put on a good show. Put on a good show and receive that money. They used to come... I think during that time to see the show was... I think it was fifty cents, or seventy-five cents, something like that. And the main thing to have the people come in there, we had to make that parade round about two or three o'clock in the afternoon.
This would be during the week or on Saturdays?
Any time. Any time.
Whatever you were doing?
Moore (I) - 27

Any time. Any time that show would come in town, we'd make the parades. We had a comedian who sat on a car, and we'd go downtown, play a (?) brief chorus... We used to (?) on the subway, and we used to go downtown. There was a place called the (?) at 125th Street; that was downtown for us, you know. We used to go downtown and circle around on the corner. That's when the band paraded, the band started playing.
I see. Well, how long were you with A.G. Allen's Minstrels?
I was with them about... I'd say about four months.
About four months. And...
Then I got with another show, they called it Old Kentucky Minstrels.
The Old Kentucky Minstrels.
Minstrels.
I see. Well, before we move on to them, where did A.G. Allen's Minstrels play? Did they play right in North Carolina, or...?
They played all over. All over. All the different spots in North Carolina, like Durham, Washington, Newborn, all the larger places. They had their own tent.
Moore (I) - 28
I see. And they would just come into a town and go out to maybe an old ball-field...?

Yeah. You'd have to... When they came in town, the first thing they'd do, you had to find out if the place is large enough. Say, for instance, if...like the guys played ball right here... We liked to play ball at the (?) places they played ball... You had to get a permit to make the parade downtown. For instance, I think it was $2.50 for your permit.
I see. That's a pretty reasonable price. While you were with A.G. Allen's, all that you did was pretty much the walking gent.
Yeah.
I see. So you didn't play any music.
Not until I was round about...oh, about six... About six months later.
You said you joined the Old Kentucky Minstrels after about four months. So this would be sometime, I guess, around 1915.
Yeah. Something around there.
You were still maybe about fourteen years old.
Yeah.
And how long were you with the Old Kentucky Minstrels?
Moore (I) - 29
The Old Kentucky Minstrels... I'd say about two months.

Uh-huh. I was playing washboard playing drums and her singing. And recently I've been doing the same thing now with Cathy Chamberlain. I've got a big book about that thick with all the pictures and all the names. I've got a big drum ...(?)... with an automobile on top of it.
I see... Well, okay... How did you get with Cathy Chamberlain, who a writer has called here "the queen of Rag-and-Roll"? How did you meet up with her and start playing?

Well, somebody had told her about me. The people she wanted to use had let down... I think they hadn't worked together or something. She had one or two (?) who was talking about who was who, how likely to work with me, and what they're going to open up with and what was they
Moore (III) - 90
going to do, you know... So we got together and had a rehearsal at some studio she rented out. She rented a studio on 45th Street and Eighth Avenue. We had a rehearsal two or three times.

We made this Rag-and-Roll Revue. She named it the Rag-and-Roll Revue, but she... She featured me a whole lot, you know. And in fact, we... We didn't record it, but we were working on stage, we worked together. We'd do things like, oh, let's see... "Jelly-Roll"... Like, "I ain't gonna do ...(?)... my jelly-roll" just by myself. And what else ....(?). Oh, "All Of Me." But anyway, she was doing things where we worked together. She'd sing one chorus of it and I'd sing the second chorus, then I'd sing the third chorus, but I put a little punch-line into the song that... That wasn't the name of it. I just put that punch-line there. "Flat-foot floogie with the floy joy," I'd put that in there.

In other words, she is a stylist who, even though she is a young woman, in her early thirties now, and at the time, in '76 or '78, she was singing music hearkening back to the 1920's, and she admires Bessie Smith and Ma Rainey and early Victoria Spivey and Ida Cox and those people...
Moore (III) - 91

Well, she... See, I know the difference. I met her... I got her a job where she is now, at Jimmy Ryan's. She's down at Jimmy Ryan's now. She's got seven pieces down there. I got her that job, and helped her get the men together, you know.

And in fact, she wanted me... I'm the first one she called to go down there and work with her. I was working down there on Saturday night with Bob Catwell(?) and His Seven Saturday Night Stompers. I was working with him. And he told the boss. He said, "Well, I think Freddie's too good. He's taking all the glamour(?) from you, and you won't..." If Freddie gets on it, gets back there with you, they ain't gonna pay you no mind -- they're going to look at him. So he says, "No, it's not a good idea; let Freddie stay where he is. You just go on your own." She tried her best to get me on drums. She even told the boss. She called me first. "I've got Freddie Moore on drums." "Who?" "Freddie Moore." "Oh, no, no. Don't get him. He's the main attraction Saturday night with Bob Catwell(?). You've got to take... Otherwise, you take him out of the band, or the band..." Blah-blah-blah. That's the way it went.
But she's down there now, and she's doing pretty good down there.
Moore (III) - 92

Well, we've come to the end of pretty much the main part of the interview, a lot of the chronology and your itinerary, who you played with and so forth. I would like to ask a couple of questions, however, one which we didn't touch on, and that is (except in the very beginning) your family, and your wife, and... You've lived here apparently... This is a senior citizens' building in the Bronx. How long have you been living here, and is it convenient to where you have to go to get to work sometimes?

I moved into the senior citizens' building in 1965. During '65...'64, that's when I got my leg hurt, my hip knocked out of place rather, and I was in the hospital, and I stayed in there, oh, I'd say about four or five weeks. I was all right. I wasn't all right, but they wanted to let me out after five weeks. So they kept me five more weeks before they had a place for me. They got me this place here. And one of the big head ladies down there, she got me into this place. I was the first one to move in here, in this building. That was 19-and... Well, after '65 or the first of '64, somewhere around there. And I've been here ever since.
Are there other musicians in this building, by the way?
No, I'm the only one.
Moore (III) - 93
[PAUSE]

You've been married thirty-nine years coming up, thirty-nine years the 2nd of June. Congratulations. That is an achievement in today's world, seriously... It's not easy, I'm sure, when you're married or being a musician, being an artist, being an artistic person or a person who is in the entertainment field, because you're gone off at odd hours, and if you do go on tour you're away for a while. So I think that's quite an achievement there.

There was another topic that I wanted to ask you about. That is for drummers. Drummers exert themselves a great deal when they're playing, perhaps in a different way, more than other members of the band. How have you managed to take care of your health all these years?
I think I had something to do with it. I say my...
I think you did, too!

I say my prayers every night. And I eat good food -- my wife cooks for me. Good food. And I get plenty of rest when I'm not working. And the only time I drink a little bit is when I'm working, if it's at night. The nights I'm not working, I don't drink anything at all no more, except a cola, Coca-Cola or something. And I take a little brandy once in a while.
Moore (III) - 94

But right now... I keep on saying I'm going to the doctor; I haven't gone yet. I have an allergy which is, I can't stand anybody smoking around me. It gets down in my throat, and I cough. And I'm a little bit allergic to different flowers. Different things. And when they get out in the air... When I get in a really hot place, I have to have air. Otherwise, I have to... Well, it ain't for me to say. It's for the doctor to say. The next thing to asthma...what is that...? Bronchitis. I think I have that.

Oh boy. It gets down there. Well, you mentioned to me one day last week that you had some trouble with your hip when you were young. You talked about the injury in 1965 or '66, just before you moved in here. But did you also have an injury when you were young?

Well, my hip was knocked out of place. I guess I must have been around, oh... I left when I was around fourteen. It was down there... That must have been around 1913, '11, '12, somewhere around there. I was a young boy. I got my leg, my hip knocked out of place riding a freight train. I grabbed the freight train, on the freight train what do they call the last car....
The caboose?
Yes. And I grabbed that. I caught myself on a hobo from one town to another, and got my leg caught down in
Moore (III) - 95
the...they call it a trussle...a cattle(?) car...
What do you call it?
The trestle. But I got my leg hooked down in there, and it was...
It was dislocated.

Dislocated... It broke. And I got up on that caboose... I made a mistake and stepped down in that catacomb(?) thing there, and I fell about...oh, I guess about four or five inches, or feet rather... And it was a good thing that another train wasn't behind me. I didn't fall between the tracks. I fell right on the side of them. If another train had been coming down there, it would have cut me in two. I just fell just like that.

That was round about, say, about a half-a-mile from where I lived. I had to crawl all the way back, because nobody knew where I was. I crawled from where the accident was; I crawled home a half-a-mile. It was dark, too; it must have been around six or seven o'clock at night. I could see snakes and things crawling in front of me. I had to cross a little sink-hole(?) pond and walk on a log to keep from, you know...
Then when I got there, my mother looked me, and she felt... I guess she felt sorry for me. She put me in a chair... She put me in a chair... During that time, you
Moore (III) - 96

didn't know about no doctors and all that stuff. She put me in a chair, and stood it ...(?)...(?)., put some bricks or rocks to put it up there and hold it. I stayed there I guess about a couple of months like that, and the thing just ...(?)..., you know. Right now, one of my legs is... This is the short one, this is the long one. One is about two inches shorter than the other. Instead of going like this, it tore (?) from there and stripped down in here, you know...
It overlapped,.
Yeah, it overlapped. And it grew like that. I came to New York in 19...I don't know what year it was...
Yeah. Oh, that's way late. That's round about before we got married...no, after we got married...
Well, '28 was way before you got married.
Yeah, I know. Well, this is after we got married. It must have been about '50, '55, '60, somewhere around in there...
Okay.

But anyway, I lived at 115 West 141st Street, on the fourth floor. And I got a chance to make some extra money, to go... I went to see a friend of mine. Some lady across the street from where I lived, she asked me did I
Moore (III) - 97

want to make thirty dollars. Thirty dollars. Thirty dollars then... I wasn't thinking about all the tolls that had to come out that. I had about five or six tolls that come out of that thirty dollars. I had to buy gas, you know. So I didn't want to go by myself, so I got my brother-in-law to go with me. And the stuff weighed around about...it was almost 500 pounds. There was a lot of cut glass and silver, knives and forks. She said to give it to somebody in Philadelphia. So I ended up coming back, I didn't have nothin'. All the money I had was twelve dollars.
Are there any other things that you'd like to add to this interview? We're almost finished here.

Well, I can't think of nothin' right now. I'm glad to be alive. And I'm still active on the bandstand. And I still love my drums. I could be working six nights a week if I want to, but I don't want to work six nights. Tuesday night is enough. That will keep me active, because that's all I know how to do, is play drums. Of course, I could find something else to do, you know, but I wouldn't be happy at that.
And I've been around some good bands, some good people, some good places. I had a lot of fun with Cathy Chamberlain. We played some good places. We even played
Moore (III) - 98
this place down here, at the Roseland. We played a concert there at the Roseland, 52nd Street and... I think it was the Roseland.
Yeah.

We played at the Roseland there. Benny Goodman came down to see us. They had two bands. They had another big band, a sixteen-piece band, but had us as an added attraction. We did shows in San Francisco and Chicago, Los Angeles, Buffalo, New York... Philadelphia at the Bijou Theatre.
The Bijou?

But just the material wasn't right, you know. She's a nice-looking girl, nice personality, but she had the wrong material. We ended up doing this... We made an album The Rag and Roll Revue. You've seen the album, haven't you.
I have not seen that album, yet.
I've got it in there. I made a few dollars. Like I said, I have to thank the good Lord who's kept me going.
Well, he certainly has. And at 82 years old, you'll be 83 this summer...
I'll be 83 August coming, the 12th of August. 83 years old. And every place I work, the way I carry myself, the way I know right from wrong at them different
Moore (III) - 99
clubs, what I'm supposed to do what I ain't supposed to do... I'm not afraid. I'm not an Uncle Tom. I'll just speak... I don't have much to say, but when I say it, people look at me and listen to me.

And when I worked down at the Red Blazer Number-Two with Bob Catwell(?) and His Saturday Night Stompers, I'd be treated just like I'm one of them. No problem. We had a (?) about making time...? I'm the first one there! I'll be down there round about... They don't hit until 9:30. I'm there at 7:30. I'm there before them. Because when I park... When I come up there around about a quarter of six or six o'clock, somebody's moving out of their place and I move right in. So I park, and I don't put no quarter in there. And I'm right there. And somebody will help me, one of the waitresses, to take my drums out and put them on the bandstand.

And when I go down Sunday, Sunday morning to get them... Because I don't bring them home on Saturday night because I was mugged a long time ago. I had two dollars, they took the money... They didn't beat me up or nothin'. Just took that money and they took my watch. That was about a quarter after four. From that time, I don't bring my drums home. I leave them right there, come around there at around about eleven o'clock, and pick them up and bring them
Moore (III) - 100
right here in the daytime. So I've been very fortunate. But that gave me a lesson. You have to be very careful.
Well, I'd like to thank you on behalf of the Jazz Oral History Project of the National Endowment of the Arts for granting this lengthy interview. God bless you.
Thank you very much. I'm so happy to be in a position so that I could think all those many years back.
Sure..
What I should have done is to write all them things down. But it's just better for me to think...
[ETC.]

segments.title: Opening: copyright notice and interview introduction
segments.summary: Copyright warning, then Ron Welburn opens the March 30, 1983 interview at Moore's Bronx home and asks how he is.

segments.title: Birth in Little Washington, running away at fourteen
segments.summary: Born August 20, 1900 in Little Washington, NC; he ran away at fourteen to join the A.G. Allen Minstrel Show because he loved drums, which his mother disliked; his father died when he was a baby.

segments.title: Walking gent with A.G. Allen: tending the band coats
segments.summary: Hired as a walking gent to hang up and dry the six-piece band's red parade coats, travelling by Pullman car.

segments.title: Marching-band repertoire: Sousa, rags and overtures
segments.summary: The minstrel band played marches, swung rags like Rastus on the Trombone, overtures and Scott Joplin-style numbers.

segments.title: Instrumentation of the band; Professor Booker and Jazz Curry
segments.summary: Lists the five-to-seven piece line-up and names bandleader Professor Booker and baritone player Jazz Curry.

segments.title: The Frog Pond dance hall and the name 'Jazz'
segments.summary: Moore sat in on drums at the Frog Pond; Welburn notes that a man named Jazz in about 1916 is an early use of the word.

segments.title: His mother, brothers and sisters, and father Giles Moore
segments.summary: Mother took in washing; Moore was the youngest of five children; he names his brothers and father and says no sibling played music.

segments.title: Little Washington and nearby North Carolina towns
segments.summary: He explains the town name and lists nearby North Carolina cities.

segments.title: Hootie Green and the Frog Pond in Newbern
segments.summary: As a boy he sat in on drums with the Frog Pond's resident pianist Hootie Green, and recalls the lack of bars.

segments.title: Cakewalks he remembers from boyhood
segments.summary: Asked about cakewalk contests, he recalls only the tune 'Cakewalking Baby'.

segments.title: Moore's trust in his memory; leaving school after third grade
segments.summary: He insists he tells the truth, then explains he left school after third grade and loved the sound and rhythm of drums.

segments.title: Homemade drumsticks from chair rungs
segments.summary: He whittled broken chair rungs into drumsticks, with no idea about rolls.

segments.title: Drumstick types, woods and prices, then and now
segments.summary: Compares old military sticks with modern plastic-tipped ones; pine, maple and hickory; price per pair; early lack of wire brushes.

segments.title: Making and warping of drumsticks
segments.summary: Some drummers made their own sticks from limbs with resin; modern sticks warp and are tested on a counter.

segments.title: Calfskin drumheads and mounting them
segments.summary: Early heads were calfskin sold unmounted; Moore describes taping and tucking heads onto the rim himself.

segments.title: Early drum kit: 28-inch bass drum, alligator pedal, no hi-hat
segments.summary: He describes drum boxes, big bass drums, alligator pedals, a single small cymbal, and not knowing hi-hats until New York.

segments.title: Bass drum technique: two beats versus four
segments.summary: Explains playing two beats for the first half-chorus then four, with an off-accent on the bass drum to make the band swing.

segments.title: Joining A.G. Allen: pay and life on the Pullman car
segments.summary: The show was a mile and a half from home; he started at three dollars a week with room and board on the car.

segments.title: A.G. Allen the man; parades and touring North Carolina
segments.summary: Allen was easy to get along with, wanted a good show; parades drew crowds; the tent show played North Carolina towns and needed parade permits.

segments.title: Leaving Allen for the Old Kentucky Minstrels
segments.summary: After about four months, still not playing, he moved to the Old Kentucky Minstrels in the Carolinas to move up toward New York.

segments.title: Joining a road show in Birmingham (TOBA-type circuit)
segments.summary: Explains 'road shows' as touring revues of musicians and entertainers, which he picked up in Birmingham.

segments.title: Becoming the drummer on the Old Kentucky Minstrels
segments.summary: When the drummer fell ill he played parade and show, was offered the job at six dollars, and describes life on the car.

segments.title: Old Kentucky Minstrels: management and South Carolina towns
segments.summary: One man was manager and boss; the show played mostly South Carolina, and the band began to play more modern, swinging material.

segments.title: Jim White, the contortion drummer
segments.summary: The drummer he replaced juggled and tossed sticks; Moore learned to use nine sticks from him, and explains the showmanship demanded of drummers.

segments.title: Where the band sat; piano or banjo in minstrel shows
segments.summary: The band sat on a platform before the stage, with a piano if there was a girl singer.

segments.title: Clarence Muse and the Charleston Dandies at Birmingham's Gaiety Theatre
segments.summary: He quit his show in Birmingham, joined Clarence Muse and the Charleston Dandies, and was housed by the theatre boss at the Gaiety.

segments.title: With William Benbow at the Frolic Theatre; backing the blues queens
segments.summary: With Benbow's company at the Frolic, aged seventeen or eighteen, he accompanied Bessie Smith, Ida Cox, Ma Rainey and other blues singers before 1920.

segments.title: Havana, then quitting in Detroit and forming a band at the Savoy
segments.summary: After Cuba he left the show in Detroit and led a seven-piece band at the Savoy for about six months (Welburn's note: Chilton dates it 1927-28).

segments.title: What a minstrel show involved
segments.summary: Describes blackface comedians, bands in minstrel shows including Freddy Jenkins and the DeParis brothers, pay, Pullman cars and railroad siding fees.

segments.title: End of first session
segments.summary: Welburn stops the first session after an hour; second session begins April 5, 1983.

segments.title: Benbow's show goes to Havana after the storm
segments.summary: Moore's third departure from Birmingham led to Benbow's show in Havana's Tropical Gardens just after a destructive storm.

segments.title: The Havana troupe and the interpreter
segments.summary: He recalls the cast of chorus girls and soubrette, hiring an interpreter, a day off Sunday, and a few Spanish words.

segments.title: Cuban musicians, music and the theatre schedule
segments.summary: Cubans admired American musicians; their music was big-band marches, calypso and rhumbas; he worked two shows a day confined to the theatre.

segments.title: Back to the States via Cleveland and Detroit's Graystone
segments.summary: After about three months in Cuba the show returned, stopping in Detroit's Graystone Ballroom.

segments.title: Florida, Louisiana and meeting King Oliver at the Graystone
segments.summary: His Florida work was with Oliver; he met Oliver in 1928-29 when Oliver's band and Jean Goldkette's shared the Graystone; Benbow's revue was the Get Happy Revue.

segments.title: Charlie Creath's four-piece band at the Kahoken Roadhouse
segments.summary: After leaving Benbow in St. Louis he played an after-hours roadhouse with trumpeter Creath for $25 a week plus tips.

segments.title: East St. Louis roadhouse and the stockyard
segments.summary: Clarifies the Kahoken was in East St. Louis by the stockyards; Creath played five nights a week there.

segments.title: How he joined and left Creath; back to Birmingham
segments.summary: Creath asked him to stay on, he left after six months when the Birmingham theatre owner sent railroad fare.

segments.title: His first band: the seven-piece group at Detroit's Savoy
segments.summary: He led a seven-piece band playing stock arrangements of tunes like China Boy and Tiger Rag for about a year before moving to New York.

segments.title: First days in New York: meeting Chick Webb, Cozy Cole, Krupa
segments.summary: He met Chick Webb, Cozy Cole, Gene Krupa and young Buddy Rich, and recalls Cozy in a dime-a-dance band.

segments.title: First lodgings and impressions of New York
segments.summary: He roomed on 129th Street for eight dollars a week and says New York lived up to what he was told.

segments.title: Drum solos: Krupa and Sid Catlett
segments.summary: He dislikes taking solos; Krupa soloed and Sid Catlett was a great drummer working on the snare.

segments.title: Buddy Gilmore and press-roll drumming
segments.summary: Gilmore gave Moore work on Long Island and was a Baby Dodds-like drummer; Moore discusses press rolls and a Gene Krupa award signed for Zutty Singleton.

segments.title: First New York job through Gilmore
segments.summary: His first New York job, five dollars a night on Long Island, came via Buddy Gilmore.

segments.title: Wilbur Sweatman and the Lafayette Theatre
segments.summary: Sweatman played several horns at once in a trio at Harlem's Lafayette Theatre; scale was $55 a week.

segments.title: Eubie Blake's fourteen-piece pit band
segments.summary: He also played in the pit for Eubie Blake's shows with changing tempos, alongside Sweatman's stage act.

segments.title: Sweatman's career and what he asked of Moore
segments.summary: Sweatman was strong in the Twenties, declined afterward, did not sing, and wanted drum solos from Moore.

segments.title: Eubie Blake as strict bandleader; the Pie, Pie Blackbird film
segments.summary: Blake was busy and strict; the band toured theatres and made a short film with Nina Mae McKinney.

segments.title: Rehearsals and tempo changes in Blake's band
segments.summary: Two-hour rehearsals and shifting waltz, foxtrot and one-step tempos under Blake's baton; popular dances included rhumba, foxtrot, tango.

segments.chapter: King Oliver, own trio and Kirby
segments.title: King Oliver's 1929-30 Victor recordings
segments.summary: Welburn and Moore sort out personnel and tunes for Oliver's Victor sessions, including that Moore played on 'Too Late'; Carroll Dickerson led the band.

segments.chapter: King Oliver, own trio and Kirby
segments.title: How he came to join King Oliver through Dave Nelson
segments.summary: Moore played the Nest Club with Dave Nelson, Oliver's nephew, who introduced him; Oliver ran a business-like band, 1929 to about 1937.

segments.chapter: King Oliver, own trio and Kirby
segments.title: Oliver's gum trouble, mutes and plunger
segments.summary: Oliver's pyorrhea forced him to use extra trumpeters and soft muted playing; Moore says he was first to use a bottle as a wah-wah mute.

segments.chapter: King Oliver, own trio and Kirby
segments.title: Trumpeters in Oliver's band: Red Elkins
segments.summary: Moore recalls second trumpeter Red Elkins from Washington as staying almost to the end.

segments.chapter: King Oliver, own trio and Kirby
segments.title: Own trio at the Victoria Cafe and Brickwood, then John Kirby's band
segments.summary: He led a trio with Pete Brown and Don Frye at Harlem cafes until Kirby hired all three at the Onyx Club.

segments.chapter: King Oliver, own trio and Kirby
segments.title: Chronology of the trio and the 101 Ranch
segments.summary: Welburn corrects Chilton's dates; Moore adds the 101 Ranch before the Onyx.

segments.chapter: King Oliver, own trio and Kirby
segments.title: The Rhythm Club and the Big Apple
segments.summary: The Rhythm Club was the musicians' hiring hall where Moore got jobs; pay varied by band size; the Big Apple was just a hangout.

segments.chapter: King Oliver, own trio and Kirby
segments.title: Trio repertoire at the Victoria: In the Mood and Swing
segments.summary: The Moore-Brown-Frye trio played Benny Goodman material and Swing tunes, with Brown on alto and Frye on piano.

segments.chapter: King Oliver, own trio and Kirby
segments.title: Meeting Erskine Hawkins in Birmingham
segments.summary: Moore met Hawkins in Birmingham before he left there.

segments.chapter: King Oliver, own trio and Kirby
segments.title: Playing in Kirby's first band at the Onyx Club
segments.summary: About two years at the Onyx, Kirby listened to sidemen, would not allow sit-ins, rehearsed, and played from memory calling keys.

segments.chapter: King Oliver, own trio and Kirby
segments.title: Learning to read; the drummer's job
segments.summary: He learned to read drum parts about a year after joining Oliver; a drummer must keep good time and make the band happy; his showmanship now.

segments.chapter: King Oliver, own trio and Kirby
segments.title: End of second session; start of third (April 10, 1983)
segments.summary: Welburn closes the second session and opens part three on April 10, 1983.

segments.title: Writing and rehearsals in the Oliver band
segments.summary: Dave Nelson wrote the arrangements; the band rehearsed at Lafayette Hall twice a week for a month; Oliver used three trumpets.

segments.title: What Oliver said of New Orleans: Keppard and Bolden
segments.summary: Oliver talked mainly about Freddie Keppard and admired Buddy Bolden's style.

segments.title: Baby Dodds as a drummer
segments.summary: Moore and Dodds drank and talked drums; Dodds had his own style with rim work and press rolls and little cymbal.

segments.title: Jean Goldkette's band and Chauncey Morehouse in Detroit
segments.summary: Moore remembers only Chauncey Morehouse from Goldkette's band, barely knew Goldkette, and did not know Trumbauer.

segments.title: Richard Chetman not recalled
segments.summary: Moore cannot place Richard Chetman, named in Chilton.

segments.title: The trio at the Victoria Cafe: no rehearsals, Pete Brown's playing
segments.summary: The trio never rehearsed; Brown played around melodies; the 105-seat cafe had a tiny dance floor.

segments.title: Dances and dance tunes at the Victoria
segments.summary: Popular numbers included Stardust and Sweet Georgia Brown; people danced the Charleston, rhumba and Black Bottom.

segments.title: Ella Fitzgerald, Big Joe Turner and Basie men sit in at the Victoria
segments.summary: Ella sang A Tisket A Tasket, Turner and Basie band members sat in from the nearby Woodside Hotel.

segments.title: Jo Jones and other visiting drummers
segments.summary: Moore rarely talked with Jo Jones; visiting drummers were wary of his wild multi-instrument solos.

segments.title: Drum styles of the era: Walter Johnson and Cozy Cole
segments.summary: Asked about stylistic differences, Moore praises Walter Johnson's hi-hat work with Fletcher Henderson and Cozy Cole's tom-tom playing.

segments.title: Cozy Cole's 24-inch cymbal and big bass drums
segments.summary: Cole gave him a 24-inch crash cymbal; Moore recalls huge bass drums, Zutty Singleton's and the show drummer Battleaxe's pedal.

segments.title: Cymbal and drum makers: Turkish, Zildjian, Ludwig, Slingerland
segments.summary: Moore moved from Turkish cymbals to Zildjians and uses Ludwig drums.

segments.title: The Kirby band: length, personnel and dates
segments.summary: About two years at the Onyx with Frankie Newton and Buster Bailey; Leo Watson replaced them; the band did not record under Moore.

segments.title: Leaving Kirby; Kirby as a bandleader
segments.summary: The band was a clique; Kirby lacked experience with keys, let sidemen dictate the drum backing, and played string bass at the Onyx.

segments.title: Rehearsals and hours at the Onyx Club
segments.summary: Rehearsals were afternoon; music ran from eight or nine until two-thirty; sit-ins happened at Jimmy Ryan's next door.

segments.title: Jimmy Ryan's on 52nd and 54th Street
segments.summary: Moore clarifies which Ryan's he means and mentions five years there with Tony Parenti after the war.

segments.title: Onyx schedule and union scale
segments.summary: Six nights a week; scale about $125 in the top union bracket.

segments.title: Depression pay with Oliver and recording scale
segments.summary: Oliver's men got $40 a week out of which they paid room and board; recording scale was $20 for four sides.

segments.title: Recording habits with Oliver
segments.summary: Takes ran three to four hours, unpaid overtime; Oliver preferred to rehearse in the studio.

segments.title: Victor's studio and the Frederick Brothers booking agency
segments.summary: Victor was near 45th and 6th; Frederick Brothers booked Oliver and had him record before touring; Moore had his own agent for his trio.

segments.title: Oliver's road boy, laundry and uniforms
segments.summary: A road-boy paid by the sidemen handled laundry; the band wore tuxedos in places like Fort Worth.

segments.title: Rooming houses and drinking-musician reputation in Fort Worth
segments.summary: Hotels were scarce; landlords disliked musicians' late hours.

segments.title: Segregated eating on the road and in Birmingham
segments.summary: He describes taking food out, back-door service, soul food in Birmingham and the Palm Beach Hotel.

segments.title: Mixed audiences and the second balcony
segments.summary: Black patrons sat in the second balcony, leading Welburn to mention 'Second Balcony Jump'.

segments.title: Kirby's quiet leadership; Moore's return to the Victoria and Edgar Hayes
segments.summary: Kirby was quiet while sidemen ran the band; after leaving he went back to the Victoria, then the Brickwood, with Edgar Hayes broadcasting from the Victoria.

segments.chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
segments.title: Start of tape four
segments.summary: Tape change; Welburn resumes with questions about the Victoria.

segments.chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
segments.title: At Johnson's trio at Kelly's Stables
segments.summary: Tenor player At Johnson hired him through the Rhythm Club for six months at Kelly's Stables at $40 a week.

segments.chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
segments.title: Early 1940s: the Playhouse
segments.summary: Brief stint at the Playhouse near the Savoy site in the early 1940s.

segments.chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
segments.title: Playing with Art Hodes at McKinley Hall; the first Blue Note record
segments.summary: He worked club dates at McKinley Hall and recorded St. James Infirmary for Blue Note with Hodes and Max Kaminsky.

segments.chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
segments.title: Between the Victoria and Hodes: the Nest with Dave Nelson
segments.summary: In the gap years he worked at the Nest with Dave Nelson.

segments.chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
segments.title: World War One draft: put in a cage as a supposed slacker
segments.summary: In Birmingham he was displayed as a slacker, then found too young for the first war and too old for the second.

segments.chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
segments.title: Hodes trio at the Village Vanguard; Blue Note sessions
segments.summary: With Hodes and Kaminsky at the Vanguard; recorded Blues and Booze, getting two percent royalties.

segments.chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
segments.title: The September 1945 pick-up session with 'Wingy' Mesheux
segments.summary: Moore identifies the trumpeter as a New York dentist with an artificial hand called Wingy.

segments.chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
segments.title: October 1945 Hodes Hot Five with Bechet and Wild Bill Davidson
segments.summary: Welburn lists the Blue Note date; Moore recalls Davidson in uniform, his side-mouth embouchure, and the Vanguard succession.

segments.chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
segments.title: Giving Bechet a job at the Circle Ballroom
segments.summary: Bechet could not get a cabaret card, so Moore hired him in his band at a taxi-dance hall, where Bechet could not read stocks.

segments.chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
segments.title: Bechet in Brooklyn; rehearsals and Jimmy Ryan's
segments.summary: Moore rehearsed with Bechet at his Brooklyn apartment, with Bob Wilber on clarinet.

segments.chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
segments.title: Unrecalled 1945-47 broadcasts with Bechet and others
segments.summary: Welburn asks about Boston and New York broadcasts; Moore does not recall them.

segments.chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
segments.title: Bechet's Blue Note Jazzmen and Columbia sides
segments.summary: Welburn lists more Bechet sessions; Moore remembers Tiger Rag, Tin Roof Blues and Sister Kate.

segments.chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
segments.title: Recording technology: Victor with Oliver versus Blue Note
segments.summary: With Oliver his drums were muffled with a handkerchief and partitions; Blue Note let him play freely.

segments.chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
segments.title: Alfred Lion and the Blue Note studios
segments.summary: Lion and Francis Wolff were nice to him; Moore remembers the office and where they recorded.

segments.chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
segments.title: Working for Bechet: tempo and swing
segments.summary: Bechet kept one steady tempo and could make any drummer swing.

segments.chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
segments.title: Pops Foster
segments.summary: They got along; Foster slapped his bass and swung.

segments.chapter: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note
segments.title: Drum and bass interplay with Clinton Walker and John Kirby
segments.summary: With Walker he used hand signals to hold tempo; Kirby tended to pull the tempo back.

segments.chapter: Postwar Chicago, Janis and De Paris
segments.title: Wilbur De Paris and Bob Wilber
segments.summary: Moore played with De Paris later at Ryan's, and with Wilber in Boston in 1948.

segments.chapter: Postwar Chicago, Janis and De Paris
segments.title: Max Roach and Kenny Clarke, the younger drummers
segments.summary: Moore considers Max Roach the top bop drummer, never copying anyone, and met him around 1929 by his reckoning.

segments.chapter: Postwar Chicago, Janis and De Paris
segments.title: Bebop sounded like 'scrambled eggs'
segments.summary: He found Parker, Gillespie and Monk's music different but still real music.

segments.chapter: Postwar Chicago, Janis and De Paris
segments.title: Chicago's Blue Note with Art Hodes; George Brunis forces him out
segments.summary: With Hodes's eight-piece band he was dismissed after eight weeks when George Brunis objected to him singing Ugly Child; Zutty Singleton followed and was also fired.

segments.chapter: Postwar Chicago, Janis and De Paris
segments.title: Red Saunders and Jazz Limited with Bill Reinhardt
segments.summary: He visited Saunders's breakfast dances then spent two years at Jazz Limited, playing washboard, singing and drums.

segments.chapter: Postwar Chicago, Janis and De Paris
segments.title: Chicago blues and a working drummer's routine
segments.summary: He did not get to know the rhythm-and-blues drummers because of his work schedule.

segments.chapter: Postwar Chicago, Janis and De Paris
segments.title: Conrad Janis's Tailgate Jazz Band on Circle
segments.summary: Back in New York he recorded for Rudi Blesh's Circle label in 1950-51, including Down By The Riverside vocal.

segments.chapter: Postwar Chicago, Janis and De Paris
segments.title: Rudi Blesh and Moore's first vocals
segments.summary: Blesh chose him to sing because of his preacher-like voice and was easy to work for.

segments.chapter: Postwar Chicago, Janis and De Paris
segments.title: Tiger Rag snare blowing and the march medley
segments.summary: He blew against the snare on Tiger Rag; the band had a New Orleans march feel.

segments.chapter: Postwar Chicago, Janis and De Paris
segments.title: Brief dance tour with Jelly Roll Morton
segments.summary: About three weeks with Morton's eleven- or twelve-piece band in Florida and the East, for about $40.

segments.chapter: Postwar Chicago, Janis and De Paris
segments.title: Joining Wilbur De Paris: rehearsals and Atlantic records
segments.summary: De Paris rehearsed twice a week for two months at Ryan's before the 1952 Atlantic recordings.

segments.chapter: Postwar Chicago, Janis and De Paris
segments.title: Rhythm section with De Paris and being let go
segments.summary: The band got along, but Moore was replaced because they wanted a New Orleans drummer; he declined to return after Zutty's brief stint.

segments.chapter: Postwar Chicago, Janis and De Paris
segments.title: De Paris band's end and Ryan's move to 54th Street
segments.summary: The band never toured and Ryan's moved from 52nd Street, lasting about a year before closing.

segments.title: Joining Mezz Mezzrow's 1954 European tour
segments.summary: Moore replaced Zutty with Mezzrow, playing washboard, drums and vocals at the Olympia in Paris.

segments.title: The tour route across Europe and North Africa
segments.summary: The band played Belgium, Switzerland, Holland, Spain, Morocco, Algeria, Libya and Italy.

segments.title: Mezzrow, Sammy Price's tour and Paris pay
segments.summary: Mezzrow was well connected but weak on clarinet; Moore later toured with Sammy Price; he earned $400 a week plus expenses.

segments.title: Mezzrow tour personnel and Jazz Limited
segments.summary: Moore moved between Chicago and Paris tours with Archey, Pops Foster and Lee Collins who fell ill.

segments.title: Mezzrow's Paris recordings, Panassie and Claude Bolling
segments.summary: Welburn lists the sessions; Hugues Panassie sent for them and Claude Bolling mimicked many pianists.

segments.title: Paris as headquarters; musicians knew everything about him
segments.summary: Based in Paris, Moore found French musicians knew his recordings and career in detail.

segments.title: Sammy Price's Bluesicians recordings in Paris
segments.summary: They discuss the Dec 1955 to Feb 1956 Paris dates and Moore's vocals.

segments.title: A rest after the tour and hazy late 1950s
segments.summary: He took a rest after Europe and cannot recall what he did next.

segments.title: Tony Parenti at Jimmy Ryan's and being let go
segments.summary: Parenti's band with Max Kaminsky and Bobby Pratt was dismissed at Ryan's around 1968-70.

segments.title: Freelancing in the 1960s
segments.summary: He freelanced around New Jersey and did no other work.

segments.title: Roy Eldridge at Ryan's: never played with him
segments.summary: He corrects Chilton: he only sat in with Eldridge at Ryan's.

segments.title: Afraid of going out at night in New York
segments.summary: He avoids going out at night now.

segments.title: Graham Stewart and the Curtain Call and Gas House gigs
segments.summary: Small low-paid gigs with trombonist Graham Stewart.

segments.title: Penn State and Victoria Spivey
segments.summary: He played washboard and drums with Victoria Spivey at Penn State.

segments.title: Cathy Chamberlain and the Rag-and-Roll Revue
segments.summary: He joined her revue after rehearsals and got her the Ryan's job.

segments.title: Moving to the senior citizens' building in the Bronx
segments.summary: He moved in 1965 after a hip injury and hospital stay.

segments.title: Thirty-nine years of marriage
segments.summary: Welburn congratulates him on his marriage of nearly 39 years.

segments.title: Staying healthy as a working drummer
segments.summary: Prayer, good food, rest, little drinking; he suspects bronchitis and allergies.

segments.title: Hip dislocated riding a freight train as a boy
segments.summary: He crawled home half a mile after a freight-train accident; the leg healed shorter.

segments.title: A thirty-dollar delivery trip to Philadelphia
segments.summary: A story of a hauling job for a neighbor that netted him almost nothing.

segments.title: Closing reflections and Chamberlain's tours
segments.summary: He is glad to be alive and active, and recalls the Roseland concert, national tours and the Rag and Roll Revue album.

segments.title: Age, dignity and the Red Blazer; being mugged
segments.summary: At 82 he says he is no Uncle Tom, describes working the Red Blazer and leaving drums there after being mugged.

segments.title: Thanks and goodbye
segments.summary: Welburn thanks him; Moore regrets not writing his memories down.
